description: document.documentURI — full URL including fragment; canonical DOM XSS source
document.baseURI — affected by <base href> which can itself be a sink
document.URLUnencoded — legacy IE property; same role as document.URL but without percent-encoding
document.location read without a sub-property — PortSwigger calls this out separately. Look-aheads exclude assignments and the already-covered sub-property reads.
window.location read without a sub-property. Same caveats as document_location_bare.
window.name — cross-origin writable; an attacker can iframe the target and pre-set this. Often missed by scanners.
history.pushState(...) — third arg becomes part of the URL; treat reads of location.* afterwards as tainted in single-page apps
history.replaceState(...) — same reasoning as pushState
new URL(location, ...) — the parsed URL inherits taint from location

searchParams.get(name) — chained (urlObj.searchParams.get), destructured (searchParams.get), or short-name (params.get / usp.get) form. NOTE: matching ".params" / ".query" by name has FP risk; agent should confirm the binding came from URL/URLSearchParams.
new URLSearchParams(...).get(...) — captures the chained call form on the same line
localStorage["key"] — bracket-access form not covered by .getItem regex
sessionStorage["key"] — bracket-access form
localStorage.key(i) / sessionStorage.key(i) — used to enumerate; values are still attacker-influenced
IndexedDB.open(...) — values stored in IDB are persistent and attacker-influenced (stored DOM XSS vector)
event.data — payload from a postMessage / WebSocket / EventSource / BroadcastChannel callback. NOTE: high false-positive rate outside event handlers; pair with handler-registration rule.
event.origin — used in postMessage origin checks; value comes from the sender, useful for finding missing origin validation
WebSocket .onmessage handler — server-pushed data is attacker-controllable when the server is compromised or speaks a third-party protocol
new EventSource(url) — SSE; same reasoning as WebSocket
new BroadcastChannel(name) — receives messages from same-origin contexts (incl. potentially compromised iframes)
XMLHttpRequest.responseText — server response data, tainted if it ever reflected user input
XMLHttpRequest.responseXML — same reasoning as responseText
XMLHttpRequest.response — when responseType is set; generic catch-all
fetch(...).then(r => r.text()|r.json()) — body of a fetch response is server data that may reflect user input
Express req.query — query-string values, attacker-controlled
Express req.body — POST/PUT body, attacker-controlled
Express req.params — URL path params, attacker-controlled
Express req.headers — request headers, attacker-controlled (incl. Host, X-Forwarded-For)
Express req.cookies — cookie values, attacker-influenced
Next.js / App-Router searchParams or nextUrl — request URL access in server components / route handlers
process.env.X — config-controlled but flagged by some rulesets when reaching dangerous sinks (Dasty paper, semgrep server-side)
process.argv — CLI argument source; attacker-controlled in CLI tools
JSON.parse(...) — when fed an attacker-controlled string, the resulting object can contain a "__proto__" key that gets walked by recursive merge functions
qs.parse / querystring.parse — these libraries historically created __proto__ keys from URL query strings (CVE-2017-1000048 family)
